x.t: Giant arms catch a spaceship back from space
b: A giant spaceship called Starship flew around Earth about 14 times. On Saturday, it came back to Texas.
Huge arms on the launch tower caught it in the air. It was the first catch of a [[starship|Starship]] back from circling Earth.
The rocket's bottom part, the [[booster|booster]], was not caught. It came down in the sea. A rocket that is caught can fly again.

o.t: SpaceX catches a Starship back from orbit for the first time
b: SpaceX, a rocket company, caught its [[starship|Starship]] spaceship in mid-air on Saturday 14 November, Texas time. Giant mechanical arms on the launch tower at Starbase, in South Texas, grabbed it. It was the first time a Starship returning from [[orbit|orbit]], a path around Earth, had been caught.

The ship lifted off on Friday on the 15th Starship test flight. It circled Earth about 14 times and released 26 [[satellite|satellites]], machines that travel around Earth. Its [[heat-shield|heat shield]], which protects it from heat on the way down, was reported to be in good shape.

The [[booster|booster]], the lower part that lifts the rocket off the ground, was not caught. It steered away from the tower and came down in the Gulf of Mexico. SpaceX had planned to catch both parts. A rocket that is caught can be used again.

stories.think: If something you tried half worked and half failed, would you call it a success? Why?

quiz.q: What caught the Starship spaceship when it came back?
a: A huge net on a boat
Giant arms on the launch tower

x.t: Why India remembers Birsa Munda today
b: Today is Janjatiya Gaurav Divas in India. It remembers [[tribe|tribal]] [[freedom-fighter|freedom fighters]].

The date is the birthday of [[birsa-munda|Birsa Munda]]. He was born on 15 November 1875. Back then, Britain ruled India. He led a big group of people against that rule. He stood up for the rights of tribal people.
The state of [[jharkhand|Jharkhand]] began on this date too, in 2000. Birsa Munda's birthplace is in Jharkhand.

o.t: Why 15 November is Janjatiya Gaurav Divas
b: Today, 15 November, is observed across India as Janjatiya Gaurav Divas. The day remembers [[freedom-fighter|freedom fighters]], people who struggled for freedom, from India's [[tribe|tribal]] communities. A tribe is a community that shares ancestors, a language and customs. The Union Cabinet, the group of senior ministers in India's national government, approved the day on 10 November 2021.

The date was chosen because it is the birthday of [[birsa-munda|Birsa Munda]]. He was born on 15 November 1875 at Ulihatu, in what is now [[jharkhand|Jharkhand]], and belonged to the Munda tribe. At that time Britain ruled India. He led a movement, meaning many people working together for a change, against British rule and for the rights of tribal people.
Jharkhand shares the date. It was separated from the state of [[bihar|Bihar]] and became India's 28th state on 15 November 2000. So its statehood day falls on Birsa Munda's birthday.

stories.think: Whose story from your own town, village or family do you think more people should know?

quiz.q: Whose birthday is on 15 November, the date of Janjatiya Gaurav Divas?

x.t: The big climate meeting reaches its halfway point
b: A meeting about [[climate-change|climate change]] is halfway through. It is called [[cop|COP31]]. It is in Antalya, Türkiye.
The team running the talks has shared a first [[outline|outline]] of a possible final agreement. An outline lists the main points.
Two of the biggest questions are still open. One is about money to help countries. The other is about [[fossil-fuels|coal, oil and gas]]. The talks are due to end on 20 November.

o.t: COP31 at halfway: a first outline, and big questions left
b: The United Nations (UN) climate summit, [[cop|COP31]], has reached its halfway point. This big meeting of countries is taking place in Antalya, Türkiye, from 9 to 20 November. The presidency, the team that runs the talks, has shared a first [[outline|outline]] of a possible final text. An outline lists the main points, so it is not yet a draft, a first full version.
Big subjects are still undecided. One is [[fossil-fuels|fossil fuels]]: coal, oil and gas. Another is climate finance, the money that helps countries deal with [[climate-change|climate change]].

At the last summit, COP30, countries agreed to at least triple [[adaptation|adaptation]] finance by 2035. Adaptation means preparing for the effects of a changing climate. Countries have not yet settled how to measure that money. The UN says that even tripled, it would cover less than a third of what developing countries need. Those are countries with less money.

stories.think: When a big group has to agree on one plan, what helps everyone feel that the plan is fair?

quiz.q: What has the team running the COP31 talks shared?
a: A finished agreement signed by every country
A new map of the world
A first outline of a possible final agreement

x.t: India sells a record amount of goods to the world
b: India sells things it makes and grows to other countries. These are called [[exports|exports]]. In October, India sold more goods than in any month before.
India also buys things from other countries. These are called [[imports|imports]].
In October, India still bought more than it sold. That gap is called a [[trade-deficit|trade deficit]]. One reason is that oil has become costlier.

o.t: India's goods exports set a monthly record in October
b: India's [[exports|exports]], the goods and services it sells to other countries, reached 89.99 billion US dollars in October. That is about 30 per cent more than in October 2025, when the total was 69.27 billion. The commerce ministry gave the figures on Friday 13 November.
Goods are things that are made or grown. Services are work done for others. Goods exports were 49.47 billion dollars, the highest monthly figure on record. Services exports were 40.51 billion.

India's [[imports|imports]], what it buys from abroad, came to 110.07 billion dollars, so it bought more than it sold. That gap is called a [[trade-deficit|trade deficit]]. It shrank to 20.09 billion dollars, from 25.15 billion a year earlier. Imports cost more partly because [[crude-oil|crude oil]], oil as it comes from the ground, has become costlier. India imports about 85 per cent of its oil.

stories.think: Look around your home. Which things do you think were made in India, and which came from another country?

quiz.q: What do we call the things a country sells to other countries?

x.t: Portugal agrees to protect a huge part of the sea
b: Portugal's government has agreed to create a huge new [[marine-reserve|sea reserve]]. It is in the Atlantic Ocean, between Madeira and mainland Portugal.
It covers about 173,000 square kilometres. Under the water are mountains called [[seamount|seamounts]]. [[coral|Corals]] and sponges live there in cold, deep water.
The government says careful fishing will be balanced with protecting nature. Portugal wants to protect 30% of its sea by 2028.

o.t: Portugal approves a vast reserve to protect underwater mountains
b: Portugal's Council of Ministers, the group that leads the government, approved the creation of a new [[marine-reserve|marine reserve]] on 12 November. That is an area of sea where nature is protected. It covers about 173,000 square kilometres of the Atlantic Ocean.

It takes in the Madeira-Tore [[seamount|seamount]] complex, a group of underwater mountains between [[madeira|Madeira]] and mainland Portugal. It protects deep-sea [[habitat|habitats]], the homes of living things. These include sponges, cold-water [[coral|corals]], which are small sea animals, and threatened species, meaning kinds of living things at risk of disappearing.

The government says it will balance protecting nature with sustainable traditional fishing, meaning fishing that does not take too much. The reserve will raise the protected share of Portugal's waters to about 25%, Reuters reports. Portugal's target is 30% by 2028. The United Nations goal is at least 30% of the world's oceans by 2030.

stories.think: If you could protect one wild place, on land or at sea, which would you choose and why?

a: Rivers that flow into the ocean

x.t: Five new kinds of small frog found in India
b: Scientists have found five new [[species|kinds]] of small frog in India. They were found in Arunachal Pradesh, in the eastern [[himalayas|Himalayas]].
They belong to a group called horned frogs. One of them eats snails. It is the first frog known in India to do that.
The team worked outdoors for five years. People living nearby helped. One frog is named after the Tanii community.

o.t: Scientists name five new horned frogs from Arunachal Pradesh
b: Scientists have named five new [[species|species]] of small horned frogs from Arunachal Pradesh, in India's eastern [[himalayas|Himalayas]]. A species is one kind of living thing. The team came from the University of Delhi and Harvard University. Sonali Garg led the research, and S D Biju is a co-author, one of the study's writers.

The discovery followed five years of [[fieldwork|fieldwork]], which means studying nature outdoors. The results appeared in Royal Society Open Science, a [[journal|journal]]. That is a magazine where researchers share their findings. The frogs belong to a group named Jingophrys, and the find more than doubles its number of known species.

One of them, Jingophrys tanogogo, is the first frog known in India to eat snails. Local communities supported the work, and some species are named for them. The Tanii horned frog's name joins the Tanii community's name with an Apatani word for frog.

stories.think: Why might it matter to people when an animal is named after their community?

quiz.q: One of the new frogs is the first known in India to eat which food?

x.t: Email stopped for many people around the world
b: On Thursday, email stopped working for many people around the world. They use Outlook, an email service from a company called Microsoft. Some work apps had problems too.
A break like this is called an [[outage|outage]]. It lasted more than a day. Microsoft said the fault came from earlier work to upgrade its [[network|network]].
Microsoft said sorry. On Saturday, it said the service was working again.

o.t: Microsoft says email outage is over after more than a day
b: Email and work apps stopped for many people around the world on Thursday 12 November. The problem affected Microsoft 365, a set of online tools. They include Outlook email and the Teams app for calls, meetings and chats. Businesses and governments were hit. A break in a service like this is called an [[outage|outage]].

The outage lasted more than 24 hours. Microsoft said the fault was introduced during an earlier upgrade to its [[network|network]], a system of computers linked together so they can share information. It showed up after a later network change. The company said it was not a [[cyberattack|cyberattack]], which is an attempt to break into computer systems to cause harm.
Microsoft apologised on Friday. On Saturday 14 November, it said service had been restored. The company has promised a full report once it has reviewed what went wrong.

local.IN: In India, email support for customers of the airlines IndiGo and Air India was affected.

stories.think: If email and messaging apps stopped for a day, how would you get an important message to someone?

quiz.q: What did Microsoft say caused the outage?
a: A fault from an earlier network upgrade
A power cut in one city

x.t: India's President gives awards to top sports players
b: On Friday, India's [[president|President]], Droupadi Murmu, gave out the National Sports Awards. The [[arjuna-award|Arjuna Award]] honours top players. It went to 17 of them.
They play many sports, like chess, [[kabaddi|kabaddi]], rowing and hockey. Divya Deshmukh and Vidit Gujrathi play chess. Tejaswin Shankar does athletics.
Nobody got the top award, the Khel Ratna, this time. Coaches, who train players, got the Dronacharya Award.

o.t: 17 sportspeople receive the Arjuna Award from the President
b: India's [[president|President]], Droupadi Murmu, presented the National Sports Awards on Friday 13 November. The ceremony was held at [[rashtrapati-bhavan|Rashtrapati Bhavan]], the President's official home. The [[arjuna-award|Arjuna Award]], which honours top players, went to 17 sportspeople.

They come from many sports. Divya Deshmukh and Vidit Gujrathi are chess players, and Tejaswin Shankar competes in athletics. Others play badminton, boxing, hockey, [[kabaddi|kabaddi]], rowing and shooting. The list also includes [[para-sport|para shooting]], which is shooting for athletes with disabilities, and deaf shooting, for athletes who are deaf.

A selection committee, a group that recommends who should win, was led by a retired judge. Nobody received the Khel Ratna, India's top sports award, this time. The last year with no Khel Ratna was 2014. Coaches, the people who train and guide players, were honoured as well, with the Dronacharya Award.

stories.think: If you could give an award to someone who helped you learn a sport or a skill, who would it be, and why?

quiz.q: How many sportspeople received the Arjuna Award?

x.t: India tests an improved rocket part on the ground
b: On Thursday, India's space agency [[isro|ISRO]] tested a rocket part on the ground. Rockets are built in sections called [[rocket-stage|stages]]. This part is the third stage of the PSLV rocket.
Two earlier PSLV flights had problems in the third stage. So engineers changed its design and updated their checks.
This time, the motor was fired without flying. ISRO said the test was a success. More tests are planned.

o.t: ISRO tests new version of PSLV third stage on the ground
b: India's space agency, [[isro|ISRO]], says it successfully tested the third stage of its PSLV rocket on Thursday 12 November. A [[rocket-stage|stage]] is a section of a rocket that is dropped once its fuel is used up, making the rocket lighter. The test took place at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota.

It was a [[static-test|static test]]: a ground test in which the motor is fired without flying. The third stage is a [[solid-motor|solid motor]], which burns a solid fuel mixture packed inside a cylinder. ISRO said the test followed anomalies, meaning problems, in this stage on two earlier missions. News reports say both missions failed.

Engineers improved the [[nozzle|nozzle]], the part at the end of the motor that directs hot gas out. They also added extra sealing and updated their checks on materials and assembly. ISRO says more tests are planned once it has studied the data.

stories.think: When something you have made does not work, how do you find out what went wrong?

quiz.q: Which part of the PSLV rocket did ISRO test on the ground?

x.t: Haaland scores as Norway beat Wales
b: Norway beat Wales 3-1 at football on Saturday. The game was played in Oslo.
Erling Haaland scored Norway's third goal from a [[penalty|penalty]]. A penalty is a free shot at goal.
It was his 23rd goal in the [[nations-league|Nations League]]. No player has scored more. He has 66 goals in 60 games for his [[national-team|country's team]].

o.t: Haaland's 23rd Nations League goal helps Norway beat Wales 3-1
b: Norway beat Wales 3-1 in Oslo on Saturday 14 November. The match was part of the [[nations-league|Nations League]], a competition for the [[national-team|national teams]] of Europe. A national team is made up of players chosen to play for their country.

Norway scored first in the 59th minute and again in the 68th. The second goal came after a pass from Erling Haaland. Wales scored in the 79th minute. Then, in the 88th minute, Haaland scored from a [[penalty|penalty]]. That is a free shot with only the goalkeeper to beat, given after a [[foul|foul]], which means breaking the rules.
It was Haaland's 23rd Nations League goal, more than any other player has scored in the competition. He now has 66 goals in 60 games for Norway. That works out at more than one goal a game.

stories.think: Would you rather score the goal or make the pass that sets it up? Why?

quiz.q: How many Nations League goals has Erling Haaland now scored?

x.t: A small rocket called Electron reaches 100 launches
b: A small kind of rocket called [[electron-rocket|Electron]] was launched for the 100th time on Saturday. It took off from New Zealand.
The rocket is 18 metres tall. It carried a [[satellite|satellite]] for a company in Japan.
The satellite makes pictures of Earth using [[radar|radar]]. Radar can see through clouds. It can see at night too.

o.t: Small Electron rocket makes its 100th launch from New Zealand
b: A rocket called [[electron-rocket|Electron]] made its 100th launch on Saturday 14 November. It lifted off at 6.30 pm local time from the [[mahia-peninsula|Māhia Peninsula]] in New Zealand. Electron, from the company Rocket Lab, is 18 metres tall.

It carried a [[satellite|satellite]], a machine that travels around Earth, for the Japanese company iQPS. The satellite, YAMATSUMI-II, went into [[orbit|orbit]], a path around Earth, about 575 kilometres up. It pictures Earth using [[radar|radar]], which sends out radio waves and reads the ones that bounce back. So it can see through cloud and at night.

Electron first flew in 2017. That test flight failed, and the first success came in January 2018. Rocket Lab says Electron reached 100 launches faster than any other commercially developed rocket, meaning one developed by a business. This was its 11th launch for iQPS, which plans a group of about 36 radar satellites.

stories.think: If you could take a picture of any place on Earth from space, at any time, what would you look at and why?

quiz.q: How many Electron launches have there now been?

x.t: 570 people dress as one film hero and set a record
b: On Friday, 570 people dressed up as the same film character. His name is [[rocky-balboa|Rocky Balboa]].
They stood on the steps of a big art museum in [[philadelphia|Philadelphia]]. Each wore a black hat and grey clothes.
Everyone was counted. It was a new [[world-record|world record]]. Then the crowd ran up the steps.

o.t: 570 fans dressed as Rocky set a world record in Philadelphia
b: A crowd of 570 people set a [[guinness-world-records|Guinness World Record]] on Friday 13 November in [[philadelphia|Philadelphia]], a city in the United States. It is the record for the largest gathering of people dressed as [[rocky-balboa|Rocky Balboa]], the main character of the film Rocky.

They met on the steps of the Philadelphia Museum of Art. The costume was a black knitted hat, a grey sweatshirt and sweatpants, which are soft clothes for exercise. It also had black high-top shoes, which cover the ankle. At least 250 people were needed for the record, and more than twice that number came.
The event marked 50 years since the film came out in 1976, with the actor Sylvester Stallone. After the count was done, people ran up the museum steps.

stories.think: If your town tried to set a friendly world record, what would you choose, and who would join in?

quiz.q: How many people dressed as Rocky Balboa for the record?

starship: A very big rocket and spaceship made by the company SpaceX.
A rocket system made by the company SpaceX. It has two parts: a booster called Super Heavy at the bottom and a ship, also called Starship, on top.
orbit: The path something follows as it goes round and round a planet, moon or star.
The curved path an object follows around a planet, moon or star, held there by gravity.
booster: The bottom part of a rocket, which gives the big push to lift it off the ground.
The first, lower part of a rocket. It gives the main push at liftoff and then separates from the part above it.
heat-shield: A cover that keeps a spaceship from getting too hot when it comes back to Earth.
A protective layer on a spacecraft. It stops the craft overheating as it rushes back down through the air.
satellite: A machine sent into space that travels round and round Earth.
A machine sent into orbit around Earth or another body. Satellites are used for jobs such as communication, taking pictures and studying weather.
freedom-fighter: A person who takes part in a struggle for their people's freedom.
A person who takes part in a struggle for political freedom. In India, the term is used for people who opposed British rule.
tribe: A group of families who share a language, customs and a long history together.
A community of people who share ancestors, a language and customs.
birsa-munda: A leader of the Munda tribe who stood up to British rule in India.
A leader from the Munda tribe, born in 1875 in what is now Jharkhand. He led a movement against British rule and for the rights of tribal people.
jharkhand: A state of India. It was separated from Bihar and became a state in 2000.
bihar: A state of India. Jharkhand was part of Bihar until 2000.
cop: A big meeting where countries talk about climate change.
Short for Conference of the Parties: the United Nations climate summit, where countries meet to agree on action on climate change.
outline: A short list of the main points of a plan.
A short summary that gives the main points of a plan or a piece of writing, without the full detail.
fossil-fuels: Coal, oil and gas. People burn them to make energy.
Coal, oil and gas. Burning them releases greenhouse gases, which trap the Sun's heat.
climate-change: Earth is slowly getting warmer, and the weather is changing with it.
The long-term warming of the Earth and the changes in weather that come with it. Burning fossil fuels is the main cause.
adaptation: Changing how we do things to cope with a changing climate.
Adjusting to the effects of a changing climate, such as floods and droughts.
exports: Things a country sells to other countries.
Goods and services that one country sells to buyers in other countries.
imports: Things a country buys from other countries.
Goods and services that one country buys from sellers in other countries.
trade-deficit: When a country buys more from other countries than it sells to them.
The gap when the value of a country's imports is bigger than the value of its exports over a period of time.
crude-oil: Oil as it comes out of the ground.
Oil in its natural state, as it comes out of the ground.
marine-reserve: A part of the sea where nature is kept safe.
An area of sea that is protected by law so that the animals and plants living there are kept safe.
seamount: A mountain that sits under the sea.
An underwater mountain that rises from the ocean floor.
coral: A tiny sea animal that lives in big groups. Many kinds build a hard home.
A small sea animal that lives in large groups. Many corals build hard skeletons, which can pile up into reefs.
madeira: A group of islands in the Atlantic Ocean that belongs to Portugal.
A group of Portuguese islands in the Atlantic Ocean. The largest island is also called Madeira.
habitat: The place where an animal or plant lives.
The natural home of an animal or plant, which gives it the food, water and shelter it needs.
species: One kind of living thing, such as a tiger or a house sparrow.
A group of living things that are alike and can breed with each other. Scientists give each species a two-part scientific name.
himalayas: A range of very high mountains in Asia.
A great mountain range in Asia that includes the highest mountains on Earth.
fieldwork: Studying nature outdoors, where plants and animals live.
Research that is done outdoors in the real world, by watching and collecting information, instead of in a laboratory or office.
journal: A magazine where scientists share what they have found.
A magazine that publishes new research. Other experts usually check each study before it is printed.
outage: A time when something people use, like power or the internet, stops working.
A period when a service, such as electricity or an online service, is interrupted and does not work.
network: A group of computers joined together so they can share information.
A system of computers and other devices that are linked together so they can share information.
cyberattack: When someone breaks into computers on purpose to cause harm.
An attempt to break into a computer system illegally, in order to cause damage or harm.
president: The person who is the head of a country such as India.
The head of state of a republic, which is a country without a king or queen. India's President is its head of state.
arjuna-award: An award that India gives to top sports players.
One of India's National Sports Awards. It is given to sportspeople.
rashtrapati-bhavan: The big house where India's President lives and works.
The official home of the President of India, in New Delhi.
kabaddi: A team game where a player runs across to tag the other team and tries to get back.
A team sport in which players take turns to cross into the other team's half, tag opponents and return without being caught.
para-sport: Sport played by athletes with disabilities.
Sport for athletes with disabilities. Para shooting is the form of shooting for these athletes.
isro: The Indian Space Research Organisation, India's space agency.
rocket-stage: One section of a rocket. A rocket drops each section when its fuel is used up.
A section of a rocket. When a stage has used up its fuel it is dropped, which makes the rocket lighter and helps it reach the speed needed to circle Earth.
static-test: A test where a rocket motor is fired on the ground and does not fly.
A ground test in which a rocket motor is fired while it stays in place, without flying.
solid-motor: A rocket motor that burns a solid mixture, not a liquid.
A rocket motor in which the fuel and the oxidiser it needs to burn are mixed into a solid and packed inside a cylinder.
nozzle: The opening at the end of a pipe or motor where gas or liquid comes out.
A shaped opening at the end of a pipe or motor that directs the flow of gas or liquid coming out.
penalty: A free shot at goal in football, with only the goalkeeper in the way.
In football, a free shot at goal with only the goalkeeper to beat. It is given when a team breaks the rules close to its own goal.
nations-league: A football contest between teams from Europe.
The UEFA Nations League, a competition between the national teams of Europe.
national-team: A team of players picked to play for their country.
A team of players chosen to represent their country in matches against other countries.
foul: Something a player does that breaks the rules of the game.
An action that breaks the rules of a sport, such as tripping or pushing an opponent in football.
electron-rocket: A small rocket from the company Rocket Lab.
A rocket from the company Rocket Lab, used to carry satellites into orbit. It is 18 metres tall.
mahia-peninsula: A piece of land in New Zealand that sticks out into the sea.
A peninsula in New Zealand. A peninsula is a piece of land almost surrounded by water. Rocket Lab launches rockets from there.
radar: A tool that finds things by sending out radio waves and catching them when they bounce back.
A system that sends out radio waves and measures the ones that bounce back, to find or picture objects.
rocky-balboa: The main character in a film called Rocky. He is not a real person.
The made-up main character of the film Rocky, which came out in 1976 with the actor Sylvester Stallone.
philadelphia: A big city in the United States.
A large city in the state of Pennsylvania, in the eastern United States.
guinness-world-records: A group that keeps a list of world records and checks new ones.
An organisation that keeps a list of world records. It checks that each new record follows its rules before the record counts.
world-record: The best, biggest or fastest that anyone in the world has done.
The best result ever officially recorded anywhere in the world for a particular feat.
paris-agreement: A promise made by countries in 2015 to slow down global warming.
A 2015 agreement in which countries agreed to keep warming well below 2°C and to try for 1.5°C, with each country setting its own targets.
un: A club of almost every country in the world that works for peace and helps people.
Founded in 1945, it has 193 member countries. The Security Council is one of its main bodies.

g-starship-catch.ctx: This was the 15th Starship test flight, and SpaceX had planned to catch both the booster and the ship. The company has caught the Super Heavy booster three times before, but it had never caught a ship. AP reports SpaceX said the booster's engines stopped firing too soon on the way back down, so it steered away from the tower and came down in the Gulf of Mexico. Space.com reports a low-fuel alarm.
g-starship-catch.ask: Is it better to test new rockets by flying them often and learning from what goes wrong, or to wait until engineers are surer that everything will work?

in-birsa.ctx: The Union Cabinet approved Janjatiya Gaurav Divas on 10 November 2021, and it was marked on 15 November that year, Birsa Munda's birth anniversary. Birsa Munda, who belonged to the Munda tribe, led a movement against British rule and for the rights of tribal people. Jharkhand, where he was born, was separated from Bihar and became India's 28th state on 15 November 2000.
in-birsa.ask: Is a national day of remembrance the best way to keep a historical figure's story alive, or do school lessons, museums and local traditions do more?

g-cop31.ctx: COP31 runs in Antalya, Türkiye, from 9 to 20 November, and the presidency's first outline of a final text is not yet a real draft. At COP30, countries agreed to at least triple adaptation finance by 2035, but they still disagree on how to measure it, including the starting figure to count from. UN News reports that tripling would meet less than a third of what developing countries need; Climate Home News, citing a UN report, says about a third.
g-cop31.ask: When countries cannot agree, is it better to accept a weaker agreement that everyone signs, or to hold out for a stronger one that might not be agreed at all?

in-exports.ctx: India's overall trade deficit, which counts goods and services together, narrowed to 20.09 billion dollars in October from 25.15 billion a year earlier. The deficit for goods alone moved the other way: IANS and Reuters report it widened to 39.88 billion dollars from 30.21 billion in September. IANS links this to costlier crude oil and shipping; Reuters also points to festive-season gold buying. India imports about 85 per cent of its oil.
in-exports.ask: Is a trade deficit always a problem for a country, or can buying more than it sells be fine if the things it buys help it to grow?

g-portugal-reserve.ctx: The reserve includes an underwater area called Gorringe, about 22,900 square kilometres in size and about 200 km off the coast. Reuters reports that the reserve will raise the protected share of Portuguese waters to about 25%, against a national target of 30% by 2028. Portugal is also working towards a United Nations goal of protecting at least 30% of the world's oceans by 2030.
g-portugal-reserve.ask: Should fishing be allowed inside a marine reserve as long as it is done carefully, or should some parts of the sea be left completely alone?

in-hornedfrogs.ctx: The five species belong to the horned frog group Jingophrys, and the study in Royal Society Open Science more than doubles the number of known species in that group. The team from the University of Delhi and Harvard University made the discoveries after five years of fieldwork in Northeast India. Local communities supported that work, and some of the frogs are named for them.
in-hornedfrogs.ask: Should a new species be named after the people and communities who helped to find it, or should its name describe the animal itself?
jobs: Herpetologist (a scientist who studies frogs and reptiles)

g-msoutage.ctx: The fault centred on Exchange Online, Microsoft's cloud email service (one that runs on the company's computers and is reached over the internet), so features that depend on it were hit while others kept working. Those affected included government bodies in Japan and Britain's NHS health service. Microsoft said the issue was introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade and surfaced after a recent network change, and it has promised a full report after its review.
g-msoutage.ask: When so many organisations rely on one company's online tools, should they also pay for a backup from a different company, even if it costs more and is rarely needed?

in-sportsawards.ctx: India's National Sports Awards honour players and coaches: the Arjuna Award goes to sportspeople and the Dronacharya Award to coaches. This time the 17 Arjuna awardees came from sports that include chess, kabaddi, rowing, para shooting and deaf shooting. UNI and PTI report that no Khel Ratna was given, and that the last year without one was 2014.
in-sportsawards.ask: Should a country's top sports awards go mainly to people who win the biggest medals, or also to people who help a less well known sport to grow?

in-pslv-test.ctx: The PSLV, or Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle, has four stages, and its first and third stages use solid motors. ISRO's statement speaks only of anomalies in the third stage on the PSLV-C61 and PSLV-C62 missions. Spaceflight Now and The Week reported in January 2026 that both missions had failed, and that the 16 satellites on PSLV-C62 did not reach orbit, the path a satellite follows around Earth.
in-pslv-test.ask: After a rocket has failed, should a space agency stop all flights of that rocket until every planned test is finished, or fly again once the main fix has passed a ground test?

g-haaland.ctx: Haaland also made the pass for Norway's second goal, so he had a part in two of the three. His 66 goals in 60 games for Norway work out at more than one a game. Norway had lost to Wales when the two teams met in October.
g-haaland.ask: Is a great goalscorer better judged by the records they set, or by how much they help their team to win?

g-electron100.ctx: Electron first flew in 2017, and its first successful flight came in January 2018. It can carry up to 300 kilograms, and Rocket Lab says it reached 100 launches faster than any other commercially developed rocket. This mission was named The Mountain God Rises, and its radar satellite can picture the Earth by day, at night and through cloud.
g-electron100.ask: Radar satellites can picture any place on Earth at any time and in any weather. Is that mostly a good thing, or should there be rules about who may take and use such pictures?

g-rocky.ctx: The film Rocky came out in 1976, with the actor Sylvester Stallone, and this gathering marked 50 years since then. At least 250 people were needed for the record, and 570 took part on the steps of the Philadelphia Museum of Art. AP reports that people ran up the steps after the record was confirmed.
g-rocky.ask: Is a record for the largest dress-up gathering a real achievement, like a sporting record, or is its value mainly in bringing people together for a day?

bigStory.t: Can the world agree to slow climate change?
bigStory.sub: COP31, the United Nations climate summit in Türkiye

x.why: Almost 200 countries are in one place to decide how to stop Earth getting too warm. What they agree will shape the world you grow up in.

o.why: Almost 200 countries are in one place to decide how to turn climate promises into action. What they agree, or fail to agree, will shape the world you grow up in.

days.o: COP31 opened in Antalya, a city on Türkiye's coast. In an unusual setup, Türkiye is the host while Australia leads the negotiations.
days.x: The big meeting began in Antalya, a city by the sea in Türkiye. Türkiye is the host, and Australia is leading the talks.

days.o: UN Secretary-General António Guterres urged leaders to get serious. A UN report projects about 2.6°C of warming this century on current promises, well above the Paris Agreement goal.
days.x: The leader of the United Nations asked every country to get serious. A report says Earth is on track to warm more than countries promised.

days.o: Leaders gather today and tomorrow. Organisers call this the implementation COP: less about new promises, more about keeping old ones. The United States did not send officials.
days.x: Presidents and prime ministers arrive today. This meeting is about keeping old promises, and less about making new ones.

days.o: On the first day of speeches, UN chief António Guterres said the climate crisis is outrunning us. Türkiye asked countries to back a voluntary pledge to raise electricity's share of the world's energy use from about 23 per cent to 35 per cent by 2035. The head of the European Commission backed it. Others want it to say the electricity must be clean.
days.x: Leaders gave speeches. The head of the United Nations said the world must move faster. Türkiye asked countries to run more cars, homes and factories on electricity.

days.o: Leaders gave their speeches and went home. At least 14 countries have publicly backed the electricity pledge, by one news site's count, and a climate fund announced 94 million dollars to help developing countries electrify. But a fund for Pacific islands and a fund for tropical forests are still short of their targets, and countries still disagree about money for adapting to climate change. In week two, negotiators must agree a final text. The summit is due to end on 20 November.
days.x: Leaders gave their speeches and went home. Some countries promised to run more things on electricity. Others asked for more money to help. Next week, countries must agree on a plan.

learn.link: From the horned frogs story, set in the eastern Himalayas

b: Earth's outer layer is broken into huge pieces called plates. The plates move very slowly, only a few centimetres a year.
Where two plates push together, the ground can fold and rise. Over a very long time, this makes mountains. The Himalayas were made this way.
Mountains wear down too. Water, wind and ice break the rock and carry the bits away.
x.remember: Mountains rise where Earth's plates push together. Water, wind and ice slowly wear them down.
x.q: What can happen where two plates push together?

o.t: How are mountains made, and how do they wear down?
b: Earth's outer layer is broken into large slabs called tectonic plates. They move slowly, at average speeds of a few centimetres a year.

Where two plates push together, the crust, the rocky outer layer, can fold and be forced upward. Mountains made this way are called fold mountains. The Himalayas rose where the Indian plate collided with the Eurasian plate. The collision began about 40 to 50 million years ago. The Himalayas are still rising: sources give rates from about 7 millimetres to more than 1 centimetre a year.
Mount Everest, in the Himalayas, is the highest mountain in the world, at about 8,849 metres above sea level. The rock at its very top is limestone that formed on an ancient sea floor.

Mountains wear down as well. Weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces. Erosion is when water, wind or ice carry those pieces away. Rivers carry the pieces, and minerals from the rock, down to the sea.
o.remember: Colliding plates push mountains up. Weathering breaks rock down, and erosion carries the pieces away.
o.q: What is the difference between weathering and erosion?
a: Weathering carries rock away, and erosion breaks it down

backThen.t: Intel announces its first microprocessor, the 4004
backThen.o: On 15 November 1971, the company Intel announced a new chip, the 4004, in an advertisement in a publication called Electronic News. The 4004 was a microprocessor, which is a computer's processor built onto a single chip. It grew out of work for Busicom, a company that made calculators. Intel says the chip held 2,300 transistors, which are tiny switches, and was about the size of a little fingernail.
backThen.x: On this day in 1971, a company called Intel showed the world a new computer chip. It was called the 4004. It grew out of work for a company that made calculators.
backThen.why: Intel says engineers could buy the 4004 and program it for many different devices. A microprocessor is the kind of chip that does the main work inside a computer.

hiddenWords.o: Satellite comes from the Latin word satelles, which means an attendant: someone who escorts or follows an important person. A satellite follows a planet around in the same way.
